## Overview

`faSummary()` extracts, rotates and summarises the **factor analytic variance
structure** of an ASReml-R V4 mixed model. For every `fa()` term in the random
formula it returns the genetic covariance and correlation matrices, the rotated
loadings, the specific variances, the variance accounted for, and — unless
switched off — the genotype BLUPs and factor score EBLUPs.

It is the engine underneath the rest of the factor analytic machinery in
**biomAid**: [`fastIC()`](fastIC.html) calls it to obtain the loadings and
scores it needs for FAST and iClass metrics, and `randomRegress()` calls it on
the FA path. Anything those functions know about the FA structure, they learned
here.

`plot_faSummary()` provides five diagnostic plots:

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `"VAF"` | Stacked 100% bar chart of variance accounted for, per environment |
| `"heatmap"` | Genetic correlation between environments, optionally clustered |
| `"loadings"` | Correlation-scaled loadings as vectors, one panel per factor pair |
| `"regress"` | Genotype BLUPs against environment loadings; slope is the factor score |
| `"added"` | As `"regress"`, with the other factors projected out |

> **Where to go next.** This vignette is about the variance structure itself.
> For selection tools built on top of it — Overall Performance, stability and
> interaction classes — see
> [Factor Analytic Selection Tools: FAST and iClass](fastIC.html).

---

## Mathematical Framework

### The FA(k) covariance structure

An FA($k$) random structure models the $t \times t$ genetic covariance matrix
across $t$ environments as

$$
\mathbf{G} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Psi},
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times k}$ holds the loadings
(element $\lambda_{rj}$: factor $r$, environment $j$) and
$\boldsymbol{\Psi} = \operatorname{diag}(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_t)$ is the diagonal
matrix of **specific variances** — the environment-specific genetic variance
not shared through the common factors. The genetic correlation matrix is
$\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{cov2cor}(\mathbf{G})$.

The attraction of the structure is parsimony: $t(k+1)$ parameters instead of
the $t(t+1)/2$ of an unstructured model, while still permitting a different
genetic variance in every environment and a different correlation between
every pair.

### Rotation

The decomposition is identified only up to an orthogonal rotation: for any
orthogonal $\mathbf{R}$, $(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{R})(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{R})^\top = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\top$.
`faSummary()` resolves this by rotating with the right singular vectors of
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ and negating, and then applies **the identical rotation
to the factor scores**. The loadings and scores therefore stay conformable and
their product is invariant.

After rotation the first factor typically captures the dominant
**non-crossover** genotype × environment interaction, with all-positive
loadings; higher factors are bipolar and carry the crossover signal. The sign
of each factor is arbitrary but reproducible.

### Correlation-scaled loadings

Dividing each row of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ by that environment's total genetic
standard deviation gives

$$
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\!*} = \operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_t^{-1}\bigr)\boldsymbol{\Lambda},
\qquad \sigma_j^2 = \textstyle\sum_r \lambda_{rj}^2 + \psi_j,
$$

returned as `loads_cor`. Each row now lies **inside the unit hypersphere**,
which is what makes the `"loadings"` plot interpretable: an environment's
distance from the origin is the proportion of its genetic variance explained by
the plotted factors, and the angle between two environment vectors approximates
their genetic correlation.

### Variance accounted for

With $\sigma_j^2$ as above, the proportion of environment $j$'s genetic
variance attributable to factor $r$, and the residual specific proportion, are

$$
\text{VAF}(r,j) = \frac{\lambda_{rj}^2}{\sigma_j^2}, \qquad
\text{Specific}(j) = \frac{\psi_j}{\sigma_j^2}, \qquad
\sum_{r=1}^{k}\text{VAF}(r,j) + \text{Specific}(j) = 1 .
$$

These are the rows of `vaf_env`. Pooling across environments gives
`vaf_summary`, $\overline{\text{VAF}}(r) = \sum_j\lambda_{rj}^2 / \sum_j\sigma_j^2$,
and `vaf_total` is the overall percentage explained by all $k$ factors
together.

> **Specific variances are clamped at zero for the VAF calculation only.**
> ASReml-R can return a fractionally negative boundary estimate for $\psi_j$,
> which would otherwise produce a negative proportion. `spec_var` always
> reports the unclamped estimate, so a negative value there is informative and
> is not hidden.

### Common variety effect

The factor score EBLUPs $\hat{\mathbf{F}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$
(element $\hat{f}_{rg}$: factor $r$, variety $g$) combine with the loadings to
give the FA regression prediction, the **common variety effect**

$$
\widehat{\text{CVE}}(g,j) = \sum_{r=1}^{k}\lambda_{rj}\hat{f}_{rg},
\qquad \widehat{\mathbf{CVE}} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\top .
$$

This is the quantity the `"regress"` and `"added"` plots decompose, and the
basis of every metric in [`fastIC()`](fastIC.html).

## Worked example — 50 Varieties × 12 Sites

> **Requires:** ASReml-R V4. The vignette is pre-rendered so no licence is
> needed to read it; run the code chunks only if you have the packages
> installed.

### Data simulation

We use the same simulated MET as the
[FAST and iClass vignette](fastIC.html) — 50 varieties at 12 balanced sites,
with a deliberately wide genetic correlation range (`g_cor_min = 0.10`,
`g_cor_max = 0.65`) so that higher factors carry real crossover signal. Using
the same data makes the two vignettes directly comparable.

```{r sim1}
#| cache: true
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
set.seed(101L)
sim1 <- simTrialData(
  nvar        = 50L,
  nsite       = 12L,
  nrep        = 3L,
  G           = "auto",
  incidence   = "balanced",
  seed        = 101L,
  verbose     = FALSE,
  sim.options = list(
    g_cor_min     = 0.10,
    g_cor_max     = 0.65,
    sigma_genetic = 300,
    error_sd      = 280,
    site_mean     = 4500,
    site_sd       = 450
  )
)
dat1         <- sim1$data
dat1$Site    <- factor(dat1$Site)
dat1$Variety <- factor(dat1$Variety)
dat1$Rep     <- factor(dat1$Rep)
dat1$Row     <- factor(dat1$Row)
dat1$Column  <- factor(dat1$Column)
```

### Fitting the FA(3) model

```{r fit1}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: sim1
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| results: hide
m1_fa3 <- asreml(
  yield  ~ Site,
  random = ~ fa(Site, 3):Variety + at(Site):Rep,
  data   = dat1,
  maxit  = 30L
)
m1_fa3 <- update(m1_fa3)
```

### Calling `faSummary()`

With `term = NULL` — the default — every `fa()` term in the random formula is
summarised. Here there is one. The `at(Site):Rep` term is not factor analytic
and is ignored.

```{r fasummary1}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: fit1
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
fas1 <- faSummary(m1_fa3)
fas1
```

The compact `print()` method reports, for each term, the number of factors, the
number of environments and the total percentage of genetic variance accounted
for. Work with the term label rather than retyping it:

```{r term1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
trm <- fas1$terms[1L]
trm
names(fas1$gammas[[trm]])
```

#### Loadings and specific variances

`loads` is the $t \times k$ matrix of rotated loadings, with columns named
`fac_1` … `fac_k`. Note the all-positive first column and the mixed signs in
the second and third — exactly the pattern described above.

```{r loads1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
g1 <- fas1$gammas[[trm]]
round(g1$loads, 2)
```

The specific variances are the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$, reported
exactly as ASReml-R estimated them:

```{r specvar1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
round(g1$spec_var, 3)
```

`Env03` is instructive: its specific variance sits on the boundary at zero, so
the three common factors account for **all** of its genetic variance — and it
has both the largest first-factor loading and the largest third-factor loading
of any site. Its `Specific` proportion in the VAF table below is therefore
exactly zero. Where ASReml-R returns a fractionally *negative* boundary
estimate, `spec_var` reports it unchanged; only the VAF calculation clamps it,
so the proportions cannot go negative.

#### Variance accounted for

`vaf_summary` pools the decomposition across environments. Shown here as
percentages:

```{r vafsumm1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
vs <- g1$vaf_summary
vs$pct_var <- round(100 * vs$pct_var, 1)
vs$cum_pct <- round(100 * vs$cum_pct, 1)
vs
```

```{r vaftotal1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
cat("Total variance accounted for by all", g1$k, "factors:",
    round(g1$vaf_total, 2), "%\n")
```

#### Genetic covariance and correlation

`Gmat` and `Cmat` are the $t \times t$ genetic covariance and correlation
matrices implied by the fitted structure. The first few sites:

```{r cmat1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
round(g1$Cmat[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

#### BLUPs and factor scores

`$blups[[term]]` holds two data frames. `blups` has one row per environment ×
variety with the BLUP, the FA regression prediction `regblup` (the common
variety effect) and `pres`, the number of non-missing observations:

```{r blups1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
head(fas1$blups[[trm]]$blups)
```

`scores` holds the rotated factor score EBLUPs in long form, with the factors
as pseudo-levels `Comp1` … `Compk` of the outer variable. `blupr` is the
rotated score; `blup` is the unrotated one:

```{r scores1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
head(fas1$blups[[trm]]$scores)
```

> Set `blups = FALSE` when only the variance structure is needed. That skips a
> potentially expensive `coef()` call, but the `"regress"`, `"added"` and
> `"loadings"` score-dependent plots then become unavailable.

---

## Visualising the structure

### Variance accounted for

The `"VAF"` plot shows, for each environment, what proportion of its total
genetic variance is accounted for by each factor and what is left in the
specific variance. Every bar reaches 100%: Factor 1 (darkest blue) at the
bottom, further factors stacked above it, and the specific variance in grey on
top. The dashed line marks the overall mean proportion explained.

Environments with a **large grey segment** are poorly described by the common
factor structure. They are worth inspecting — for outlying observations,
unusual site characteristics, or simply as candidates for an additional factor.

```{r plot1_vaf}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "VAF")
```

Environments are ordered by first-factor loading by default; `order = "asis"`
keeps the data order and `order = "cluster"` groups similar environments.

### Genetic correlation heatmap

The `"heatmap"` type displays `Cmat` on a diverging palette centred at zero.

```{r plot1_heat}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-height: 6
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "heatmap")
```

`order = "cluster"` reorders both margins by average-linkage hierarchical
clustering on $1 - \mathbf{C}$, which brings any block structure onto the
diagonal. This is usually the more informative view when looking for groups of
genetically similar environments:

```{r plot1_heat_clust}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-height: 6
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "heatmap", order = "cluster")
```

> The clustering uses `stats::hclust()`. The original `ASExtras4::fa.asreml()`
> used `cluster::agnes()`; switching to base R avoids an extra dependency for a
> purely presentational ordering.

### Correlation-scaled loadings

The `"loadings"` plot draws each environment as a vector of correlation-scaled
loadings, one panel per pair of factors — with $k = 3$ that is three panels.
The unit circle is drawn for reference. Environments reaching beyond `tol`
(default `0.85`) are drawn solid and blue; those falling short are dotted and
red, indicating that the plotted pair of factors does not explain them well.

Two readings: an environment's **distance from the origin** is how well the
pair explains it, and the **angle between two vectors** approximates their
genetic correlation — vectors pointing the same way are positively correlated,
opposed vectors negatively so, and perpendicular vectors roughly independent.

```{r plot1_loadings}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-height: 7
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "loadings")
```

Requires $k \ge 2$; it errors on an FA(1) model, where there are no pairs to
plot. Tighten or loosen the solid/dotted split with `tol`:

```{r plot1_loadings_tol}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-height: 7
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "loadings", tol = 0.6)
```

### Regression of BLUPs on loadings

The `"regress"` plot is the FA model's own interpretation of a variety's
performance: for each factor, the variety's BLUPs are plotted against the
environment loadings, and **the slope of the fitted line is that variety's
factor score**. A steep positive slope on Factor 1 is a variety that gains more
than average from favourable environments.

By default the varieties shown are each factor's extremes — the minimum and
maximum score on every factor, up to `n_varieties`:

```{r plot1_regress}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "regress", n_varieties = 4L)
```

Varieties are rows and factors are columns. Name them explicitly with
`varieties = c("Var01", "Var22")` to follow particular lines.

### Added variable plots

With $k \ge 2$ the plain `"regress"` panels are misleading: the scatter about
each line contains the other factors' contributions, so the points look noisier
than the fit really is. The `"added"` type removes them, plotting

$$
\hat{u}_{gj} - \sum_{s \ne r} \lambda_{sj}\hat{f}_{sg}
\quad\text{against}\quad \lambda_{rj},
$$

which is the correct display when more than one factor is fitted. The slopes
are unchanged — they are still the factor scores — but the points now sit
tightly around them.

```{r plot1_added}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "added", n_varieties = 4L)
```

### Returning the plotted data

Every type accepts `return_data = TRUE`, giving a list with `$plot` and
`$data` instead of the plot alone — useful for tabulating or re-plotting.

```{r return_data1}
#| eval: !expr asreml_ok
out <- plot_faSummary(fas1, type = "VAF", return_data = TRUE)
names(out$data)
head(out$data$env, 3)
```

---

## Combined `vm()` and `ide()` terms

A common MET model separates additive and non-additive genetic effects:

```r
random = ~ fa(Site, 2):vm(Variety, Ginv) + fa(Site, 2):ide(Variety)
```

Each term is summarised in its own right. In addition, when `combine.ide =
TRUE` (the default) and such a pair shares the same outer and inner variables,
`faSummary()` appends an extra entry named `"<outer>:<inner>-total"` holding the
**summed** covariance matrix and summed BLUPs — the total genetic structure.

That entry has no loadings or scores of its own, because the sum of two FA
structures is not itself an FA structure. Consequently only
`type = "heatmap"` is available for it; the other four plot types raise an
explanatory error. Pass `combine.ide = FALSE` to suppress it.

---

## Summary

### `faSummary()` arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `model` | — | Fitted ASReml-R V4 model whose random formula contains at least one `fa()` term |
| `term` | `NULL` | Character vector of FA term labels to summarise, e.g. `"fa(Site, 3):Variety"`. `NULL` summarises every FA term found |
| `blups` | `TRUE` | Return genotype BLUPs and factor score EBLUPs. `FALSE` skips the potentially expensive `coef()` call |
| `combine.ide` | `TRUE` | Append the summed `vm()` + `ide()` "total" structure where such a pair exists |

### `faSummary()` return

An object of class `faSummary` with `$gammas`, `$blups`, `$terms` and `$call`.
Each `$gammas[[term]]` contains:

| Component | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `Gmat`, `Cmat` | $t \times t$ genetic covariance and correlation matrices |
| `loads` | $t \times k$ rotated loadings (columns `fac_1` … `fac_k`) |
| `loads_cor` | Correlation-scaled loadings; rows inside the unit hypersphere |
| `spec_var` | Specific variances, **unclamped** |
| `vaf_env` | Per-environment proportions: `Factor1` … `FactorK`, `Specific`, `total_var` |
| `vaf_summary` | Pooled proportions: `factor`, `pct_var`, `cum_pct` |
| `vaf_total` | Overall percentage accounted for by all $k$ factors |
| `k`, `env` | Number of factors; environment labels |
| `outer`, `inner`, `inner_fun` | Environment variable, genotype variable, and the wrapper on it (`id`, `vm`, `ide` or `total`) |

Each `$blups[[term]]` contains a `blups` data frame (`<outer>`, `<inner>`,
`blup`, `regblup`, `pres`) and a `scores` data frame (`<outer>` holding
`Comp1` … `Compk`, `<inner>`, `blup`, `blupr`).

> `pres` counts non-missing observations per environment × genotype and is
> `NA`, not `0`, where the combination is entirely absent.

### `plot_faSummary()` arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `res` | — | An object of class `faSummary` |
| `type` | `"VAF"` | One of `"VAF"`, `"heatmap"`, `"loadings"`, `"regress"`, `"added"` |
| `term` | `NULL` | Which FA term to plot; `NULL` takes the first carrying loadings |
| `order` | `"loading"` | Environment ordering for `"VAF"` and `"heatmap"`: `"loading"`, `"asis"` or `"cluster"` |
| `varieties` | `"default"` | Varieties for `"regress"` / `"added"`; `"default"` picks each factor's extremes |
| `n_varieties` | `6L` | Maximum number selected by `"default"` |
| `tol` | `0.85` | Radius threshold flagging well-explained environments in `"loadings"` |
| `theme` | `theme_bw()` | A ggplot2 theme object |
| `return_data` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` returns `list($plot, $data)` |

### `plot_faSummary()` types

| Type | Requires | Description |
|------|----------|-------------|
| `"VAF"` | — | Stacked 100% bar chart per environment: one segment per factor plus specific variance, with a dashed overall-mean line |
| `"heatmap"` | — | Genetic correlation on a diverging palette centred at zero; the only type available for a combined `vm()` + `ide()` entry |
| `"loadings"` | $k \ge 2$ | Correlation-scaled loadings as vectors, one panel per factor pair, with the unit circle; `tol` splits solid from dotted |
| `"regress"` | `blups = TRUE` | BLUPs against loadings, faceted variety × factor; slope is the factor score |
| `"added"` | `blups = TRUE` | As `"regress"` with the other factors projected out — the correct display when $k \ge 2$ |
